rationale: B wins because it knows which angles are ready and which are still evidence-shaped holes. Its line, "Without that person this angle does not exist — do not pitch it on the feature alone," is the adult in the room; A's "it won't say how much they'll make" turns a normal launch data gap into a slightly prosecutorial headline. Both sets understand the fee, IPO, and category stories, but B's proof gates are sharper and more likely to keep a founder out of a reporter's deleted folder.
gaps_in_A: "Discord just gave server owners a way to get paid — it won't say how much they'll make" overplays the facts. The update says no earnings data exists yet because the program is new; it does not say Discord is withholding anything.

"Discord's move signals monetization is coming for the whole server, not just the streamer" makes the category thesis do more work than the evidence supports. Premium roles and content suggest community monetization, but the streamer contrast needs proof.
"how this revenue stream fits alongside existing lines (ads, Nitro)" smuggles in outside revenue context. If those lines matter, they need sourcing; they were not in the supplied facts.

The fee angle misses a hard proof question: whether the 10% is all-in, permanent, and inclusive of processing costs. "charging creators a 10% cut instead of 30%" is too clean until that is nailed down.
gaps_in_B: "direct shot at the prevailing platform-fee structure" assigns competitive intent Discord did not state. The comparison is fair; the motive needs confirmation.
"right before an IPO" overstates the timing. The facts say Discord is reportedly preparing for an IPO, not that an IPO is imminent.
"the person who has run a large gaming community for free" invents "large" and "for free." Good customer-story shape, but those details must come from the actual server owner.
"community membership becomes the product" is a strong thesis, but roles and premium content alone do not prove the model shift. It needs examples of what paid access actually unlocks.
